# Learn Rust by understanding what its compiler guarantees

Rust is easier to understand when you begin with **ownership**, not with its syntax. The compiler must know who owns a value, whether a reference may safely read or change it, and when that value is no longer valid.

The learning materials use **Rust stable 1.100.0** (released 12 November 2026) and **Rust 2024 Edition**. The concepts are illustrated with original programs that normally fit in one short \`fn main()\`.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Start here

Begin with **[Ownership](01-ownership.qmd) → [Borrowing](02-borrowing.qmd) → [Lifetimes](03-lifetimes.qmd)**. These three ideas explain a large share of Rust's surprising compiler errors.
:::

## First, understand the four kinds of access

~~~rust
fn main() {
    let mut text = String::from("hello");
    let read = &text;
    println!("{read}");      // shared read
    let write = &mut text;    // earlier read is no longer used
    write.push('!');
    println!("{text}");      // hello!
}
~~~

**What happened?** The String is still owned by \`text\`. Both references merely borrow it. Once the shared reference is no longer used, the compiler can permit a new mutable borrow. If both incompatible borrows were used simultaneously, compilation would fail. This is a *lifetime and aliasing* guarantee, not a garbage collector.

## The 16 short chapters

### 1. Values and references

1. [Ownership and Moves](01-ownership.qmd) — why \`let b = a\` moves a String.
2. [Borrowing](02-borrowing.qmd) — \`&T\` versus \`&mut T\`.
3. [Lifetimes](03-lifetimes.qmd) — why annotations do **not** extend a value's life.
4. [Slices and Strings](04-slices-and-strings.qmd) — \`String\` ownership versus \`&str\` views.
5. [Enums and Match](05-enums-and-match.qmd) — represent one of several valid states.
6. [Option, Result, and ?](06-option-and-result.qmd) — make missing data and errors explicit.
7. [Traits and Generics](07-traits-and-generics.qmd) — reusable behaviour without class inheritance.
8. [Collections and Iterators](08-collections-and-iterators.qmd) — transform values without index bookkeeping.

### 2. Memory and concurrent execution

9. [Smart Pointers](09-smart-pointers.qmd) — \`Box\`, \`Rc\`, \`RefCell\`.
10. [Thread Safety](10-concurrency.qmd) — \`Arc\`, \`Mutex\`, \`Send\`, \`Sync\`.
11. [Async/Await](11-async-await.qmd) — a Future is not a thread.
12. [Macros by Example](12-declarative-macros.qmd) — \`macro_rules!\` and token expansion.

### 3. Meta-programming, organisation and boundaries

13. [Attributes and Procedural Macros](13-attributes-and-proc-macros.qmd) — the precise answer to "custom annotations".
14. [Modules, Cargo and Tests](14-modules-cargo-and-tests.qmd) — small projects with explicit namespaces.
15. [Unsafe and FFI](15-unsafe-and-ffi.qmd) — where the compiler transfers a safety obligation.
16. [Copy, Clone and Drop](16-copy-clone-and-drop.qmd) — implicit value copies, explicit clones, cleanup.

## The special case: custom annotations

Built-in \`#[derive(Debug)]\` works in a single Rust file. But **defining a custom \`#[add_label]\` attribute needs a separate procedural-macro crate**, because it executes at compile time and emits Rust tokens. Our [two-crate example](examples/index.qmd) adds one generated function to a marked item, with no third-party dependencies.

This differs from Java's reflection-oriented annotation model: Rust attributes are not automatically runtime metadata that can be inspected through a reflection API.

## Run examples, without a framework

For most lessons, copy the \`fn main\` example to \`main.rs\`, then run:

~~~bash
rustc --edition 2024 main.rs
./main
~~~

Or use the [examples and automated checks](examples/index.qmd). The website CI compiles **each standalone chapter example** and runs the real procedural-macro project.

## How to study each page

First describe the problem in ordinary English. Then read the rule, execute the program with the shown values, and explain why an invalid variation fails. When a mathematical relation appears, the page explains every symbol and substitutes concrete values immediately afterwards.
